summary: Defines a canonical text format for writing IPv6 addresses, because the flexible forms allowed by RFC 4291 caused problems for operators and users. Implementations should write this form but still accept any legal form. It is a Proposed Standard.

eli5.summary: There are many ways to write the same address, like writing 1 or 01. This picks one standard way so everyone matches.

questions: how to write an ipv6 address
what is the canonical ipv6 text format
subtitle: One canonical way to write an IPv6 address as text, so searches, logs and diffs stop disagreeing.

tldr.problem: RFC 4291 lets one IPv6 address be written in many ways (leading zeros or not, different "::" choices, upper or lower case), which causes trouble for searching, comparing, logging and operating.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC picks one form: suppress leading zeros, use "::" to its maximum but never for a single zero field, shorten the longest zero run (the first if tied), and use lowercase hex digits.
tldr.outcome: Systems SHOULD generate this form, but all implementations MUST still accept any legitimate RFC 4291 format. The RFC updates RFC 4291.

facts.label: Leading zeros
facts.value: Suppressed; a single 0000 field is written 0

facts.label: Shortening with ::
facts.value: Never for just one 16-bit zero field

today: RFC 5952 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4291, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It sets the recommended text form while leaving every RFC 4291 form legal to accept.

sections.title: One Address, Many Spellings
sections.content:
A single IPv6 address can be written as text in many ways. The RFC lists eight spellings of one address, including 2001:db8:0:0:1:0:0:1, 2001:0db8:0:0:1:0:0:1, 2001:db8::1:0:0:1, 2001:db8:0:0:1::1 and 2001:DB8:0:0:1::1. All of them mean the same address.

This flexibility has caused many problems for operators, systems engineers and customers. The RFC describes the problems and then defines a canonical text format. It does not define a format for internal storage, such as in an application or database.
sections.eli5: It is like having eight different ways to write your home address on an envelope. They all work, but they make it hard to check that two envelopes go to the same house.

sections.title: The Flexibility in RFC 4291
sections.content:
Section 2.2 of RFC 4291 allows three kinds of variation, and this RFC points them out one at a time.

  • Leading zeros. Leading zeros in a 16-bit field need not be written, but they also need not be omitted, so 0001, 001, 01 and 1 are all possible.
  • Zero compression. The symbol :: stands for one or more groups of 16 bits of zeros. It can be used or not for a single zero field, it can cover different numbers of fields when several are zero, and since it can appear only once, there is a choice of where to place it.
  • Case. RFC 4291 states no preference between uppercase and lowercase.
sections.eli5: The old rules said you may skip the extra zeros, you may squeeze a run of zeros into two colons, and you may use big or small letters. Every one of those choices lets people write the same thing differently.

sections.title: Problems the Flexible Model Causes
sections.content:
The RFC groups the problems into searching, parsing and modifying, operating, and a few minor ones.

  • Searching. Many applications such as spreadsheets and text editors cannot search with regular expressions. If a spreadsheet holds 2001:db8::1:0:0:1 and someone searches for 2001:db8:0:0:1::1, there is no match, which can lead to an address being assigned that is already in use. The same happens with whois output and with network diagrams during troubleshooting.
  • Parsing and modifying. Every tool must parse addresses so that all forms mean the same address. Plain-text diffs of configurations show a change when only the spelling changed, and a text comparison of an X.509 certificate address can wrongly report it as invalid.
  • Operating. A system may show back a different form from the one the operator typed. Network operations staff and abuse teams must parse addresses by eye, and a mistake in the placement of :: is called critical in the abuse case.
  • Minor. Code may behave differently when moved between platforms, documents with several authors become harder to read, and capital D and 0, or capital B and 8, can be misread.

The RFC contrasts this with IPv4, where text representation has very little flexibility and addresses cannot be abbreviated.
sections.eli5: If one friend writes your phone number with dashes and another with spaces, a computer searching for one will not find the other. That is the kind of mix-up this causes, only for network addresses.

sections.title: The Canonical Text Format
sections.content:
The recommended form complies fully with RFC 4291. Systems SHOULD follow it when generating an address as text, and humans are advised to follow it too. All implementations MUST still accept and handle any legitimate RFC 4291 format.

  1. Leading zeros MUST be suppressed. 2001:0db8::0001 is not acceptable and must be 2001:db8::1. A single 16-bit 0000 field MUST be written as 0.
  2. Use :: to its maximum. 2001:db8:0:0:0:0:2:1 must be 2001:db8::2:1, and 2001:db8::0:1 is not acceptable because 2001:db8::1 is shorter.
  3. Never use :: for just one 16-bit zero field. 2001:db8:0:1:1:1:1:1 is correct and 2001:db8::1:1:1:1:1 is not.
  4. Shorten the longest run. When there is a choice, the longest run of consecutive zero fields MUST be shortened. If runs are equal in length, the first one MUST be shortened, so 2001:db8::1:0:0:1 is the correct form of 2001:db8:0:0:1:0:0:1.
  5. Lowercase. The characters a to f MUST be lowercase.
sections.eli5: The rules are: drop extra zeros, squeeze the longest run of zeros into two colons (but only if it saves something), and always use small letters. Follow them and everyone writes the same address the same way.

sections.title: Special Addresses and Port Numbers
sections.content:
Some addresses, such as IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses, ISATAP addresses and IPv4-translatable addresses, carry an IPv4 address in their low-order 32 bits. These may use mixed notation, with hexadecimal followed by dotted decimal in the last 32 bits only. Mixed notation is RECOMMENDED when the address can be recognized as embedding IPv4 from a well-known prefix alone, and MAY be used when some external method says the prefix embeds IPv4. The earlier rules still apply to the hexadecimal part, giving ::ffff:192.0.2.1 rather than 0:0:0:0:0:ffff:192.0.2.1. The RFC admits a trade-off here between exact-match searching and readability.

There are many ways to attach a port number to an address in text, such as [2001:db8::1]:80, 2001:db8::1:80, 2001:db8::1.80 and 2001:db8::1#80. The second form is the most ambiguous because of the :: syntax, and it is NOT RECOMMENDED. The bracket style from RFC 3986 SHOULD be used and is the default. URIs containing IPv6 literals MUST follow RFC 3986 as well as the rules in this document.

IPv6 prefixes should be written by the same rules as addresses.
sections.eli5: When an address has an old-style IPv4 number tucked inside, you may write that part with dots. And when you add a port, put the address in square brackets so nobody confuses the port with part of the address.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC notes that comparing IPv6 addresses as text can create a security risk if it is used for access control. Its example is the X.509 case in Section 3.2.5, and it points out that the common practice for comparing X.509 data is to do so in binary format.

In an appendix the RFC recommends that developers use display routines that conform to these rules. It says getnameinfo() with the NI_NUMERICHOST flag in FreeBSD 7.0 gives conforming output apart from the special addresses, and that inet_ntop() of FreeBSD 7.0 is a good C code reference but should not be called directly.
sections.eli5: A computer should compare the real numbers inside an address, not how it was typed. Otherwise two spellings of the same address might get treated as different, and a lock might let the wrong visitor in or keep the right one out.
